Browser basics::Command queue.summary: Cypress commands are queued for later execution and yield subjects through the command chain instead of returning values synchronously. Use chaining or `.then()` to work with a command's result.
Browser basics::Command queue.explanation: Cypress commands are added to a central queue when invoked and execute later in order. A command does not synchronously return its subject; instead, Cypress yields that subject to the next command or passes it to a `.then()` callback. Synchronous JavaScript runs immediately, so use chaining or `.then()` when code depends on a Cypress result.
Browser basics::Command queue.returns: Cypress commands return immediately after being appended to the queue; their subjects are yielded rather than synchronously returned.

example.explanation: The callback receives the subject yielded by the preceding command, so assertions or dependent work run after Cypress resolves the command.

useCases.title: Consume a yielded subject
useCases.scenario: Access the element or value produced by a previous Cypress command.

useCases.title: Sequence dependent assertions
useCases.scenario: Run assertions only after a command has resolved.

keyPoints: Cypress manages the chain and passes each command's yielded subject to the following command.
Use the yielded subject through chaining or a callback rather than expecting a synchronous return value.
Calling a command schedules it; execution happens later through Cypress's command queue.
The JavaScript call finishes immediately, while the queued command sequence executes afterward.
`.then()` receives the previous command's resolved subject as its first callback argument.
gotchas: Do not assign a Cypress command to a variable expecting its eventual subject; use chaining or `.then()` instead.
Avoid mixing immediate JavaScript reads with commands when the JavaScript depends on a command that has not run yet.
Do not treat Cypress chains as ordinary promises or try to reconcile them with your own promise flow.

Browser basics::Commands and chaining.summary: Cypress commands are queued and composed into chains, with each command yielding a subject to the next. Queries and assertions retry; action commands execute once, so re-query after DOM-changing actions when necessary.
Browser basics::Commands and chaining.explanation: Cypress queues commands while the test function runs and executes them afterward. Each command yields a subject for the next command; queries and assertions can retry, while action commands execute once, so separate queries may be safer when the application re-renders elements.
Browser basics::Commands and chaining.returns: Each command yields a subject to the next command; the yielded value depends on the command.

example.explanation: This chain queries an input, checks it, types into the yielded element, and verifies the resulting value.

useCases.title: Retryable checks
useCases.scenario: Read application state and assert that it has reached an expected condition.

useCases.title: Inspecting subjects
useCases.scenario: Pass a yielded DOM element or value into custom callback logic.

useCases.title: Stable interactions
useCases.scenario: Re-query after an action that may trigger a DOM re-render.

keyPoints: Cypress commands form chains because each command yields a subject that the following command receives.
Begin a chain with a `cy` command; the first command's yielded subject determines which commands can follow.
Queries inspect application state, yield elements or other data, and retry until the yielded result is current.
Calling a Cypress command queues it; execution happens after the test function has finished setting up the chain.
Use `.then()` to access the previous yielded subject in a callback after the preceding command resolves.
gotchas: Commands are enqueued rather than executed immediately, so do not depend on ordinary synchronous JavaScript timing around Cypress commands.

Browser basics::cy.get and querying.summary: `cy.get()` queries DOM elements by selector or retrieves aliases. As a Cypress query, it retries and yields a subject that can be chained into actions and assertions.
Browser basics::cy.get and querying.explanation: `cy.get()` queries the document for matching elements and automatically retries while Cypress waits for the application to reach the expected state. It can also resolve aliases such as `@saveButton`; the yielded subject can be used safely by later commands and assertions. When chained from `cy`, searching starts at the document, except inside `.within()`, where it starts from the scoped root.
Browser basics::cy.get and querying.syntax:
cy.get(selector)
cy.get(alias)
cy.get(selector, options)
cy.get(alias, options)

parameters.name: selector
parameters.description: A selector used to filter matching DOM elements.

parameters.name: alias
parameters.description: An alias created with `.as()` and referenced using `@` plus its name.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options that change the default behavior of `cy.get()`.

Browser basics::cy.get and querying.returns: Yields the matching DOM elements or the result of an alias lookup; for an intercept alias, yields the most recent interception or null if no request has matched. The result is safe to chain further commands.

useCases.scenario: Match several element types in one query.

keyPoints: Use `cy.get(selector)` to find one or more DOM elements, or `cy.get(alias)` to retrieve an aliased value.
Selector matching follows familiar jQuery-style querying behavior.
The selector argument filters the elements returned from the application DOM.
An optional options object can customize command behavior, such as timeout-related settings.
The yielded subject is either the matched elements or the value resolved from an alias.
Comma-separated selectors let one query return elements matching any listed selector.
gotchas: A top-level `cy.get()` searches the whole document; use `.within()` when the query should be scoped to a container.
The command yields a subject for subsequent commands, rather than performing an immediate synchronous lookup.
Alias lookups require the `@` prefix, such as `cy.get('@saveButton')`.

Browser basics::Interacting with forms.summary: Fill form controls with Cypress commands, assert their values or state, and submit the form with `.submit()`. The submission command requires the selected subject to be a `<form>`.
Browser basics::Interacting with forms.explanation: Use Cypress's DOM queries and action commands to operate form controls as a user would, then assert the resulting values or state. Submit the form explicitly with `.submit()` when the form itself is the subject.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional settings that change the command's default behavior.

Browser basics::Interacting with forms.returns: Yields the same subject it was given.

keyPoints: Call `.submit()` to submit a form selected from the page.
Select the form itself before calling `.submit()`; an input element is not a valid subject.
The command yields the original form subject, but later commands should not rely on that subject because Cypress marks such chaining unsafe.
Start the command chain with a DOM-yielding query such as `cy.get()`.
Assertions chained before submission are awaited automatically.
gotchas: Do not depend on the form subject in commands chained after `.submit()`; query the page again or assert an independent result.
`.submit()` only works when the command chain yields a form, not an input or another element.
Client-side validation failures cause `.submit()` to fail, so provide valid required values when testing successful submission.

Configuration::Fixtures and test data.summary: Load fixed test data from a file in Cypress’s fixturesFolder. Use it to share deterministic records or assets and to stub network responses without relying on a live backend.
Configuration::Fixtures and test data.explanation: Place stable test data in the configured fixtures folder and load it with cy.fixture(), or reference it directly in an intercept response. Cypress caches a fixture after its first read, so repeated uses receive the same contents; use cy.readFile() instead when a file changes during the test.
Configuration::Fixtures and test data.syntax:
cy.fixture(filePath)
cy.fixture(filePath, encoding)
cy.fixture(filePath, options)
cy.fixture(filePath, encoding, options)

parameters.name: filePath
parameters.description: Path to a file within the fixturesFolder; the extension may be omitted.

parameters.name: encoding
parameters.description: Encoding used to read the fixture, including null for a Cypress.Buffer.

Configuration::Fixtures and test data.returns: Yields the loaded fixture contents, parsed or encoded according to the file type and supplied encoding.

keyPoints: Fixtures keep controlled, reusable test data outside the test implementation.
Unless configured otherwise, Cypress resolves fixture paths from cypress/fixtures.
Use cy.fixture() to load fixed records or supported assets from the fixtures directory.
Fixture data can serve as deterministic responses for intercepted network requests.
Fixtures are intended to remain stable during execution, supporting repeatable tests.
JSON fixtures can also be imported statically when build-time loading suits the spec.
gotchas: A fixture is cached after its first read for a given path and encoding, so editing the file during a test will not change later reads.
Use cy.readFile() for generated or changing files rather than cy.fixture().
The fixtures folder must be configured for cy.fixture() to work.

Debugging::Debugging and retries.summary: Use the Command Log, snapshots, console details, and cy.debug() to inspect failed browser behavior. Enable test retries to compare repeated attempts and identify flaky tests.
Debugging::Debugging and retries.explanation: Cypress exposes each test command in the Command Log and captures snapshots that can restore the application to earlier states. Clicking a command reveals its subject and result; enabling test retries reruns failed tests for additional attempts, while cy.debug() adds a breakpoint and browser-console details for the previous command.
Debugging::Debugging and retries.syntax:
cy.debug()
retries: { runMode: number, openMode: number }
Debugging::Debugging and retries.returns: cy.debug() yields the subject received from the previous command; test retries rerun failed tests up to the configured retry count.

keyPoints: Clicking a command exposes its subject and yielded value for diagnosis.
In open mode, expand retry attempts individually to compare their behavior.
Use test retries to identify flaky tests and failures that appear in CI.
Place cy.debug() in a chain when you need a breakpoint while a linked assertion is failing.
gotchas: Test retries must be enabled in Cypress configuration before failed tests receive additional attempts.
cy.debug() does not repeatedly log or break during later retry cycles.
